query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying friction stir processing (FSP) to the surface of CoCrFeNi will refine its grain structure and induce a nanocrystalline layer that, by promoting the in‐situ formation of a continuous, self‐healing oxide glaze during sliding, will maintain a lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate from room temperature up to 800 °C compared to the untreated, coarse-grained alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a conventional coarse-grained microstructure as typically produced by casting or other standard processing.
generation.intervention: Perform friction stir processing on the CoCrFeNi surface under controlled thermal and mechanical conditions to generate a fine-grained, nanocrystalline surface layer.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding tests in air with a specified normal load (e.g., 5 N) and sliding speed, evaluated at temperatures ranging from room temperature to 800 °C. The environment, load, sliding distance, and speed are controlled to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, nanocrystalline surface layer that facilitates rapid and uniform oxidation to form a continuous oxide glaze.
generation.mechanism: FSP-induced grain refinement increases surface hardness, reducing plastic deformation and wear. The fine microstructure also promotes the formation of a stable, adherent oxide film during sliding. At higher temperatures, this oxide glaze acts as a lubricious and protective layer, countering the tendency toward increased friction and wear, while at lower temperatures the enhanced hardness reduces abrasive and adhesive wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The processed CoCrFeNi will exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and a reduced wear rate across the full temperature range compared to the unprocessed baseline. While the exact quantitative improvement is uncertain, a measurable reduction in both friction and wear under identical test conditions is anticipated.
generation.baseline: The as-received or conventionally processed CoCrFeNi alloy exhibiting coarser grains and less uniform oxide film formation during sliding.
generation.boundary: Sliding tests conducted under dry conditions in air, using a normal load of approximately 5 N and appropriate sliding speeds, with temperatures incrementally varied between room temperature and 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement (i.e., percent reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate) is not predetermined, and the stability of the nanocrystalline layer at the highest test temperatures remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi samples: one group undergoing friction stir processing (FSP) to create the refined surface and a control group in the as-received coarse-grained state. Subject both groups to identical dry sliding tests in air under a fixed normal load (e.g., 5 N) and sliding speed, with the temperature sequentially increased from room temperature to 800 °C. Measure real-time friction coefficient and post-test wear rates via profilometry and SEM analysis.
measurements: Wear track depth and volume (using 3D optical profilometry)
Microstructural characterization (SEM/EBSD) of the worn surfaces to confirm grain refinement and oxide layer formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FSP-treated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in both the average friction coefficient and the wear rate across the full temperature range compared to the control samples, or if the refined layer does not sustain its structure and protective oxide formation at high temperatures, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The tribological behavior of the samples was evaluated by reciprocating sliding friction and wear tests using a ball-type friction tester (UMT trilobal machine, Bruker, Saarbrucken, Germany). The CoCrFeMnNi HEA sample was rubbed against a hardened Si3N4 ball with a diameter of 10 mm. The hardened Si3N4 ball has excellent wear resistance, does not react with the alloy, and will not adhere to the sample surface, which ensures the stability of the friction test. All the wear tests were dry friction under different loads and sliding speeds at room temperature. The normal load of the friction test is 5 N and 30 N, the sliding speed is 1 mm/s, 5 mm/s, and 10 mm/s, the friction length is 5 mm, and the sliding time is 1200 s. The balls and samples should be cleaned with acetone ultrasonic for 20 min before each friction and wear test. In order to ensure the validity and repeatability of friction test data, each friction coefficient curve was obtained through three reciprocating wear experiments under the same condition. cited_evidence.text: This is also consistent with the previous friction coefficient data and specific wear rate data. The friction coefficient of FG sample is small, and the specific wear rate is low. Under high normal load, with the increase of sliding speed, the main wear mechanisms of the two samples are adhesive wear, oxidative wear, and plastic deformation. Compared with low loading, the phenomena of wear debris, glaze layers, and oxide layers occurred earlier. This indicates that both samples are more prone to oxidation friction under the high normal load. The oxide layer acts as a lubricating layer, resulting in a reduced coefficient of friction on the worn surface. Therefore, in the friction coefficient curve, the friction coefficient of both samples under high normal load conditions is smaller than that of under low normal load. However, the formation of the oxide layer is accompanied by the occurrence of oxidative wear, which leads to the accumulation of wear volume and the increase of specific wear rate. At this point, the oxide layer formed on the FG sample is more resistant to rupture. Therefore, the FG sample shows good wear resistance.
